<section aria-label="What happened"><p>I asked my husband Rick to try a simple search in ChatGPT. “Who is Beth Aden, and what does she do for people? bethadenai.com”</p><p>The answer described me as someone you’d hire for AI visibility audits, GEO, and AEO. I still take on select AI visibility projects. The work I do most often now is hands-on operations. I help businesses get stalled projects moving, straighten out handoffs, and build workflows, tools, and automations their teams can actually use. When a friend tried a similar search, the answer said it couldn’t find enough reliable information to explain what I did.</p><p>I kept BethAdenAI.com and used <strong>Beth Aden</strong> as the public name. I updated the site and LinkedIn around my current work, worked through domain verification, and checked the business profile and agent in ChatGPT. Each step answered a different question. Could the platform reach the site? Did it have the current information? What would someone actually see when they searched?</p><figure aria-label="Four ways customers discover a business"><ul><li><b>Google Search · SEO</b> — Help Google discover and index your pages and match them to relevant searches.</li><li><b>Google Maps · Local SEO</b> — Help nearby customers find and contact an eligible business.</li><li><b>Direct answers · AEO</b> — Answer the questions customers ask in language they can use.</li><li><b>AI search · Discovery</b> — Give tools such as ChatGPT and Claude public details they can find and check against their sources.</li></ul><figcaption>Figure 1. The website supports all four paths. Each one has its own way to check the result.</figcaption></figure></section>

<section id="baseline"><h2>Find out what customers see today</h2><p>Start in Google with your exact business name, then search your domain. If customers hire you locally, try your name and city, then your main service and city. Open the listings and links that describe you. Save the URL, the description, and anything outdated.</p><p>Next, open a fresh ChatGPT or Claude conversation with web search enabled. Start with your name and domain. Then leave your name out and ask the kind of question a customer would actually ask. Open every source that supports a claim about you. If the answer gives you no source for that claim, log it as unknown.</p><blockquote>Search the web for Beth Aden at bethadenai.com. What services does she currently offer? Cite the page that supports each service and flag anything you can’t confirm.</blockquote><blockquote>Who helps small construction companies build a job-tracking workflow so dispatch and field crews can see who owns each open work order? Find providers that work remotely and cite their service pages.</blockquote><p>The first test checks whether people can find and identify you by name. The second checks whether someone could discover you while looking for help. A good result in one tells you where to look next.</p><p><a href="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-conducting-your-searches-on-search">ChatGPT web search</a> · <a href="https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10684626-enable-and-use-web-search">Claude web search</a></p></section>

<section id="website"><h2>Put the current business on your website</h2><p>Write one plain-English description you can adapt wherever people find you. Mine would start like this. <em>I help businesses get stalled projects moving and build workflows their teams can run. That includes clearer handoffs, job-tracking systems, and coordinating launches, bids, and transitions.</em></p><p>Put that clarity on the homepage, then give each major service its own public page. Say who it’s for, what problem it solves, what the client gets, and how the work starts. On the About page, connect the person to the business and the domain. Back up what you do with selected work, a testimonial you have permission to use, or a redacted example. Make the contact link easy to find and test it on your phone.</p><p>Update the places that still describe the old offer. Check LinkedIn’s headline, About, Services, and Featured sections, along with public directories, partner bios, old author pages, and relevant listings. If an article still helps readers, keep it and update any wording that presents a retired offer as current. If you retire a page and have a close replacement, redirect readers to that replacement. Ask directory owners to correct entries you can’t edit yourself.</p><p>On each important page, use a specific title and main heading, link to it from a related page or your navigation, and write descriptive alt text for meaningful images. Put essential details in readable text on the page itself. If you add structured data, use an appropriate type and keep it consistent with what readers can see.</p><p><a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide">Google SEO Starter Guide</a></p></section>

<section id="console"><h2>Check whether Google can index your pages</h2><p><a href="https://search.google.com/search-console/">Google Search Console</a> shows how Google sees your website. It’s where you check indexing, submit a sitemap, and see search queries and pages earning impressions and clicks.</p><ol><li><strong>Add the property.</strong> Choose Domain to cover the domain and its subdomains, including <code>www</code>. Choose URL prefix to cover a specific prefix such as <code>https://www.example.com/</code>. Use an existing verified property if the business already has one.</li><li><strong>Verify ownership.</strong> For a Domain property, follow the DNS instructions Google supplies. If it gives you a TXT record, open the provider that actually manages your DNS. Your domain registrar, DNS provider, and website host can be three different companies. Add a new record and copy Google’s host and value. Your DNS editor may represent the root as <code>@</code>, a blank field, or the domain name. Check how it handles the domain before saving. Keep existing records in place. Return to Search Console and verify after DNS updates become visible.</li><li><strong>Submit your sitemap.</strong> Open <strong>Sitemaps</strong> and submit the actual sitemap URL, often <code>https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml</code>. Open it first and check that it includes the current homepage, services, and articles you want discovered.</li><li><strong>Inspect priority URLs.</strong> Paste the full homepage or service URL into <strong>URL Inspection</strong>. Compare the indexed result with <strong>Test live URL</strong> if something looks wrong. Check whether Google can fetch the page, whether indexing is allowed, and which canonical URL Google selected. For a new or materially updated page, use <strong>Request indexing</strong> when available and check back later.</li></ol><figure><ol><li><b>Business verifies the domain</b>Search Console grants access to the site’s reports.</li><li><b>Google discovers and evaluates the URL</b>The sitemap and internal links help Google find the page. URL Inspection shows its status.</li><li><b>The owner checks performance</b>Compare impressions and clicks by query and page. Track contact inquiries in your own analytics or CRM.</li></ol><figcaption>Figure 2. Verification, indexing, and earning a click are separate events. An indexing request starts a review. Inclusion is up to Google.</figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9008080">Site ownership verification</a> · <a href="https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9012289">URL Inspection</a></p></section>

<section id="maps"><h2>Set up the Google listings that fit your business</h2><p>If customers visit you or you visit them in person, search Google Maps for your business name and city. Claim the matching listing or request access if someone already manages it. If there’s no listing and you’re eligible, add your business and use the verification option Google offers.</p><div className="overflow-x-auto"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">How you work</th><th scope="col">Which setup fits</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Customers visit you</td><td>Use an eligible staffed location with a customer-facing address.</td></tr><tr><td>You visit customers</td><td>Use a service-area profile. Hide the address if customers don’t visit it.</td></tr><tr><td>Both are true</td><td>Use a hybrid profile for an eligible location and the areas you actually serve.</td></tr><tr><td>You work entirely online</td><td>Focus on your website and search visibility. Google Business Profile generally requires in-person customer contact.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>Use the real business name and a primary category that describes what customers hire you to do. Add accurate hours, contact information, services, and photos that help a customer recognize the business. If you have a storefront, show the actual entrance. Ask real customers for honest reviews and respond to them. Google describes local ranking in terms of relevance, distance, and prominence.</p><p>If you sell physical products online, check Google Merchant Center’s free listings. Submit eligible products and keep the titles, photos, prices, and availability consistent with your actual product pages. Add shipping and return details as required and check product issues in Merchant Center. For a product company, that’s a different path to discovery from the company name appearing on Maps.</p><p><a href="https://support.google.com/business/answer/7039811">Business Profile eligibility</a> · <a href="https://support.google.com/business/answer/2911778">Add or claim a profile</a> · <a href="https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091">Local ranking</a> · <a href="https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/13889434">Merchant Center free listings</a></p></section>

<section id="answers"><h2>Answer the question your customer actually asks</h2><p>SEO helps people find pages through search. AEO, or answer engine optimization, is how I think about writing a page that answers a real question clearly enough for someone to use the answer. Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode still rely on search fundamentals. To be eligible as a supporting link, a page needs to be indexed and eligible to appear in Google Search with a snippet. Google specifies no special AI schema.</p><figure><p><strong>What the customer asks</strong><br />“Can someone help us set up one place to track work orders?”</p><p><strong>What the service page answers</strong><br />“I build job-tracking workflows that show what came in, who owns it, when it’s due, and what’s holding it up.”</p><p><strong>What backs it up</strong><br />Show an anonymized tracker, explain what happens when an order stalls, and link to a relevant case study or contact page.</p></figure><p>Pull questions from sales calls, support emails, and customer conversations. Give the short answer first, then explain how the work goes, who it fits, and where the exceptions are. If a detail changes the answer, say so. For example, a product page can show the surfaces a product works on, the ones to avoid, and how to use it. A field-services page can explain service areas, the work the crew handles, and how to request a quote.</p><p>For one practical use of ChatGPT or Claude, paste public copy from a service page and three anonymized customer questions. Ask it to show which questions the page answers, cite the exact wording, and list the gaps. Add the real answers yourself and check that the page still sounds like you.</p><p><a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features">Google’s guidance on AI Overviews and AI Mode</a> · <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide">Google’s generative AI search guide</a></p></section>

<section id="ai"><h2>Check the website and the business profile separately</h2><h3>Make the public website reachable</h3><p>Ask your website manager to check <code>robots.txt</code> and any host or content delivery network restrictions. For ChatGPT search, OpenAI names <code>OAI-SearchBot</code> as the crawler to allow for inclusion in summaries and snippets. Check the homepage, service pages, and any article you want people to find. A reachable page can be considered for inclusion. Placement varies by query.</p><h3>Claim your business in ChatGPT when eligible</h3><p>Open <a href="https://chatgpt.com/business-hub">Business Hub</a>. Search for the exact business name and check the website or location before claiming a match. If there’s no match, use the add-business option when the platform offers it. Available actions vary by business type and location.</p><p>Use the verification method offered. If you choose domain verification, add the TXT record ChatGPT supplies. Keep it separate from Google Search Console’s record. Follow any identity verification and review steps in Business Hub. If an agent is available and you choose to publish it, check that it answers from accurate service, product, or policy information.</p><p>My business agent went live. I still needed a fresh customer-style search to see whether ChatGPT would describe my current services or bring my business up on its own. A published agent proves the agent is available. A cited website result, a business card, and an unprompted recommendation are three different observations.</p><p>For a broader check, run the same prompts in Claude with web search and in the other search tools your customers use. Bing Webmaster Tools also accepts sitemaps if you want to check the site’s presence in Bing. Keep the results for each platform because the sources and answers can differ.</p><p><a href="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001635-setting-up-your-business-on-chatgpt">OpenAI Business Hub setup</a> · <a href="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856">OpenAI crawler guidance</a> · <a href="https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/Sitemaps-3b5cf6ed">Bing sitemap guidance</a></p></section>

<section id="retest"><h2>Keep a record you can compare</h2><p>After a meaningful update, rerun the same searches and record the date, platform or search feature, exact query, what appeared, and which URLs were cited. Include the city if the query was local. A spreadsheet with one row per test is enough.</p><div className="overflow-x-auto"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">If you see this</th><th scope="col">Check this next</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Google can’t find the service page</td><td>Open URL Inspection and check whether Google can fetch it and which URL is canonical. Verify that the page is linked from your site.</td></tr><tr><td>An AI answer repeats a service you retired</td><td>Open the citation and find the exact wording. Update the page or request a correction. Record the source as unknown if no citation supports the claim.</td></tr><tr><td>People find you by name only</td><td>Test a specific customer problem against your service page. Add the missing answer and a real example if the page leaves readers guessing.</td></tr><tr><td>People click but never contact you</td><td>Try the next step on your phone. Check whether the offer is clear and whether the form, booking link, or checkout works.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>If you do one thing today, search your name and website the way Rick searched mine. Open the source behind what comes back. Fix the first outdated detail you can verify, then save that same search so you can run it again.</p></section>
